You’re All Delusional

It’s highly likely you need a reality check about today’s dating economy.
Take our questionnaire and find out.

To get started, answer who you are, your ZIP code, where to search, and the type of partner you are looking for.

About you: Answer as much as possible and be honest. You can skip questions about yourself, but it will make your final results and report less complete.

Your ideal match: Only set what you truly need. No preference includes everyone.

Save: Copy your code to come back later. It is labeled with the place you searched and the date and time you saved it. To pick up where you left off, paste the whole code into the second box. Older codes still load.

For more information, email colin@colinmaynard.net.

      Why we built this. Both the Manosphere and the Femosphere get the data wrong when they lob narratives at one another these days. When we dug into the viral (and admittedly intriguing) Female Delusion Calculator and heard the “I’m Looking for a Man in Finance” meme a million times, we decided it was time to put all the data on the table.

      Mutual matches. People who would date you and who also meet your expectations. “Would date you” at the top counts everyone single and not in a relationship who would date you, before your filters. The line under it shows how many of them are actively dating. Your mutual matches are the part of that group you want.

      Starting count. The Census Bureau’s American Community Survey (2020–2024) counts single people, meaning never married, divorced or widowed, by sex and age in every metro area. Every answer narrows that number.

      Not in a relationship. The Census counts people who live with a partner or are in a committed relationship as single. They come out first, in a step of their own. Pew Research Center 2022 finds about 6 in 10 unmarried adults are not in a relationship. “You’d pursue” counts only people who are not in one.

      Actively dating. Not everyone out of a relationship is dating. Checking “Only actively dating” keeps the share who say they are looking for a relationship or dates, by sex and age: about half of single men and a third of single women, from Pew Research Center 2020 and 2022. Fewer of the divorced and widowed are looking; that adjustment is our estimate. Left unchecked, every count includes everyone single and not in a relationship, and “Would date you” and your mutual matches keep the same share of them. Your rank, chance and competition always count only people who are actively dating, because they are the ones in the market.

      Local where possible. Each metro’s own Census figures for race, education, earnings, field of work, employer, citizenship, disability and same-sex couples. County rates for weight, smoking, vaping, drinking, exercise and depression (CDC), religion (US Religion Census) and politics (2024 election returns). State rates for felony records (prison data), serious mental illness and drug use (SAMHSA), and incomes above $100,000 (Census microdata).

      National where necessary. Height, past partners, wanting children, wanting to marry, relationship goals, attendance within each faith and having children come from national surveys, applied to each area’s own mix of ages, races and education.

      Traits that go together. Filters that tend to come together are measured person by person, so they are not cut as if they were unrelated. Background traits such as race, birthplace, disability, education, work and earnings come from Census records of single adults in ACS 2023 microdata. Children, body type, exercise, smoking, vaping, drinking and depression come from CDC records of single adults in BRFSS 2023. Health habits with each other come from 190,134 single adults in BRFSS 2024. Small samples count for less. Income also depends on education and age; smoking, drinking and drug use on education and religious practice; education, weight, children and religion on race.

      Who would date you. How open the people you want are to you uses what people actually do wherever that has been measured: dating-site studies for race, height, income and education, and real couples for age gaps and weight. Where only surveys exist, “would not date” answers count in full, and “less likely to date” answers count at 45% of a refusal, the ratio between what people say and what they do about smokers. Smoking itself counts in full. Your “would date you” count first removes everyone your answers rule out, at full strength (a felony, smoking or a serious illness cuts the same share at any age), then counts who is open to your age, person by person: how fast acceptance falls with the age gap comes from who actually marries whom (newlyweds in Census data), scaled so a 10-year gap is refused at the rates Pew reports (women: 27% for a man 10 years older, 42% for one 10 years younger; men: 47% and 16%); then every other answer moves it up or down against a typical competitor on the same questions, the same scores used for your rank. Height, income, education and fitness can raise it as much as weaker answers lower it. Effects combine on the odds scale, the way the dating studies measured them, so a woman already likely to say yes moves a little and one on the fence moves a lot. A skipped question counts as average. Because this page measures relationships, people who want only something casual count as matches only for each other. More past partners lowers interest for men and women alike (Stewart-Williams, Butler & Thomas 2017).

      Your competition. Your competitors are everyone of your sex who is single, dating and attracted to the people you want, at any age, counted by how much of their dating attention lands on your pool, and weighted by how sought-after your pool is, because attention flows toward the most desirable people (Bruch & Newman 2018). To measure how sought-after they are, the app asks the reverse question: how many people of your sex who are actively dating would be open to a typical person who meets your filters, compared with a typical local person. That weight is measured once for your area and kept between 0.25× and 6×. Each one is simulated from local data and scored the same way you are, on the questions you answered. Faith and race always count here, even if you skipped them. Competitors of another faith or race are less likely to chase the people you want, by the same survey figures that decide how open those people are to you. Your score out of 10 is your rank among them in tenths, rounded up. A 10 means you outrank more than 90% of them.

      Aiming high costs more. The more desirable the people you aim for, the harder they judge your weak spots, and the stronger the competition chasing them (Bruch & Newman 2018; Conley & Glauber 2007 on women’s BMI and husbands’ earnings). Four rules apply this. Aiming high: filters for high-earning, tall or degreed men, or for women 25 to 37, slim or very active, make the people you want stricter on looks if they’re men (BMI, fitness) and on status if they’re women (income, height, education). Reaching across age: when the middle of your age range is more than 8 years younger than you, the same applies, growing to full strength at 16 years. Educated targets make dealbreakers cost more (felony, drugs, smoking, not working, no degree). Devout targets make lifestyle answers cost more (casual dating, heavy drinking, marijuana, many past partners, not wanting marriage). At full strength a rule squares the penalty, so one that halved your appeal now quarters it. That strength is our estimate, not a measured figure. Combinations no study has measured, such as race and faith together, are multiplied as independent, except BMI and exercise: when both count against you, the exercise penalty counts at half strength because the two overlap, and a healthy BMI with 150+ minutes of exercise a week earns a small premium for reading as fit rather than just thin (both estimates).

      Your chances in the dating economy. The 0–100 number is your chances in the dating economy with the expectations you’ve set. A typical active dater starts from the yearly rate for their age (15 in 100 at 18–29, 23 at 30–44, 21 at 45–64, 8 at 65 and over), and your number rises or falls with how open the people you want are to you compared with your competition. Your edge is applied to the odds of that rate, so it stays realistic at both ends. The typical dater is measured nationwide, so a local market with many competitors for each person you want lowers your chance and a looser one raises it. It also falls as your filters narrow the field, including an age range narrower than the ages at least 70% of people your sex and age would date: you still meet people across the whole market, and only the ones who meet your expectations count. Online, filters steer the search and cost little; in person they cost in full. The two are weighted by how couples now meet: 39% of opposite-sex and about 65% of same-sex couples met online (Rosenfeld, Thomas & Hausen 2019).

      Operational sex ratio. Biologists call the number of men ready to mate for every woman ready to mate the operational sex ratio (Emlen & Oring 1977). It, not the total population, decides how hard each side must compete: when women are scarce, men compete harder on status and resources; when men are scarce, women compete harder on looks and commitment is harder to get (Guttentag & Secord 1983). Across history the market sorted more and more around status, wealth for men and youth and looks for women, as farming, inheritance and later cities and wages changed who could marry. Today the shortage single women feel is of economically attractive men (Lichter, Price & Swigert 2019), and on dating sites women rate most men below average while concentrating on a minority (Rudder 2014). Your local operational sex ratio counts single straight men and women who are looking. Your filtered ratio counts your competitors for the people you want. The high-status ratio counts men 27–50 who are 6′0″ or taller, not obese, earning $250,000 or more, with a bachelor’s degree, and women 25–37 (prime childbearing years; fertility declines faster after 37, per the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists) with a slim BMI (18.5–22.9), 150+ minutes of exercise a week and a high school education or less; both single, looking, with no felony, no disability and never diagnosed with depression.

      Across history. One yardstick for every era: the share of your sex left over when everyone you compete for pairs up. For past eras it comes from how many women had partners or children for every man who did: 17 to 1 in the Neolithic bottleneck (Karmin 2015), about 2 to 1 among hunter-gatherers (Wilder, Mobasher & Hammer 2004) and in polygynous societies (Henrich, Boyd & Richerson 2012), about 1 to 1 under European and industrial monogamy (Hajnal 1965), and 1.12 to 1 in the U.S. today (Census 2019). For you, it is your competitors per person you want, times how unevenly the other side’s interest is spread across your competitors, measured from the same appeal scores as your rank on every question. Past eras count who actually paired up; yours counts interest, so it shows how steep the market feels, not who will end up married.

      Precision. Every count starts from the published Census estimate and is carried through each step without rounding. Counts after the first step are estimates, so small ones also show a range. The range covers Census sampling error only, not the uncertainty in the rates applied after it.

      Known limits. Same-sex daters are judged by the preferences of the sex judging them (Bailey 1994); height has no effect for them because no study gives a usable figure for same-sex height preferences. The straight, gay and lesbian counts in the top bar include bisexual people. Puerto Rico and other territories aren’t covered. Alaska uses its statewide vote. Seven Connecticut metro areas use state religion rates because their boundaries changed after the 2020 Religion Census. Middle Eastern or North African isn’t a Census race category yet. Height, past partners and children aren’t published locally. The weight refusal figure is from 1998, validated against 2022–2023 surveys. The yearly relationship rates come from a small follow-up study. Sex is limited to the two categories the Census publishes.

      Fixes coming. Counties with prisons, military barracks, college dorms and nursing homes count those residents among local singles, so their counts run slightly high until we remove people living in group quarters. Serious mental illness, disability and felony records rest on state rates and few studies; we will add local and measured sources as they appear. The strength of the four aiming-high rules and the BMI and exercise overlap are our estimates, to be replaced with measured figures. Traits outside the Census and CDC records are linked only where noted above; the rest are multiplied as independent until measured overlaps are added. Long reports take a few seconds to build, and we are making them faster.

      What this is. An estimate of scale built from public data, not a list of real people.
